title: Compute the nth Fibonacci number, where each number is the sum of the two before it. Explain the naive recursion, why it is slow, how memoization and the bottom-up rolling approach fix it, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Fibonacci Number (Introduction to Dynamic Programming with Memoization)

s1_definition.profdef: The Fibonacci sequence defines each term as the sum of the previous two terms, with base cases of zero and one. The naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems exponentially, so dynamic programming caches each result once. Memoization stores computed values top-down, while the bottom-up form keeps only the last two values in rolling variables for constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India projects a reward-points balance that each month equals the sum of the two previous months. Instead of recomputing the whole history every time, we remember the last two months and roll forward.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each term is the sum of the previous two, so cache results and roll two values forward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Fibonacci sequence defines each term as the sum of the previous two terms, with base cases of zero and one. The naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems exponentially, so dynamic programming caches each result once. Memoization stores computed values top-down, while the bottom-up form keeps only the last two values in rolling variables for constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India projects a reward-points balance that each month equals the sum of the two previous months. Instead of recomputing the whole history every time, we remember the last two months and roll forward.

**One line to remember:** Each term is the sum of the previous two, so cache results and roll two values forward.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive recursion `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` is correct but recomputes the same calls an exponential number of times, giving order of two-to-the-n work. The first dynamic programming fix is memoization: we keep an array or map, and before computing `fib(n)` we check if it is already stored, returning the cached value if so. This turns the exponential tree into a linear number of distinct computations. The second fix is bottom-up tabulation, where we compute from the base cases upward.

The bottom-up rolling core is `int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { int cur = prev1 + prev2; prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur; } return n == 0 ? 0 : prev1;`. A concrete check: for n equal to six the sequence is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so the answer is eight. Senior nuance: memoization uses order-n time and order-n space, while the rolling bottom-up uses order-n time and constant space, which is the version to prefer when only the final value is needed and overflow is handled with long or BigInteger.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a loyalty programme where the projected reward-points target for a month equals the sum of the two previous months' targets, and analysts frequently ask for the target many months ahead. Recomputing the full chain each time is wasteful when the same intermediate months are requested repeatedly. This is exactly how the Fibonacci number works under dynamic programming: we cache each month's value once and roll forward.

The code defines a `RewardProjectionService` with `projectedTarget(month)` using the rolling bottom-up approach. A `Demo` requests a month and logs the projected target.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is month six. Step 1: we reject negatives and shortcut month zero to a target of zero. Step 2: we set the two base values, previous-two to zero and previous-one to one, representing months zero and one. Step 3: at month two the current becomes one, and we roll so previous-two is one and previous-one is one. Step 4: at month three the current becomes two, at month four it becomes three, at month five it becomes five. Step 5: at month six the current becomes eight, and after rolling previous-one holds eight. Step 6: the loop ends and we return the projected target of eight, having touched each month exactly once.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Fibonacci number is the classic introduction to dynamic programming, and I use it to show that I understand the difference between a correct solution and an efficient one. The naive recursion, where each term calls itself for the previous two terms, is perfectly correct but does an exponential amount of work because it recomputes the same subproblems over and over. The entire point of dynamic programming is to compute each distinct subproblem exactly once.

There are two standard fixes, and I explain both. Memoization keeps the recursion but caches each result in an array or map, so the second time a term is needed it is returned instantly, turning the exponential call tree into a linear number of real computations. Tabulation flips this to bottom-up: I start from the base cases and build upward, and since each term only depends on the previous two, I keep just two rolling variables and discard everything older, which gives linear time and constant space.

At the National Bank of India I applied this shape to a loyalty projection where each month's reward target was the sum of the two previous months, and analysts queried targets far into the future. I computed the value with the rolling two-variable approach and cached results in Redis so repeated queries were instant. Explaining why the naive version is exponential, how memoization and tabulation each fix it, and why the rolling form reaches constant space is exactly how I demonstrate that I understand the foundation of dynamic programming.

---

keyPoints: Bottom-up: tabulation — iterative, often more efficient
